institutionName: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I originally thought I could study oenology there, since Vienna grows wine within city limits and there were several courses about it, but it turned out those courses were in german, which I missed when I signed up.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a really great experience, but every paperwork aspect of it was very chaotic and anything but easy.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I had done a lot of research on the website in advance, so I knew pretty much everything beforehand. For me the challenging part was the application process before I arrived.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I took part in the introduction days, where everything was explained with regards to how to pick courses and what was expected of us.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Be aware that a lot of things in Austria in general requires you to book appointments in advance, show up at offices, pay with cash and that not everyone speaks english.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I had a bad experience with HousingAnywhere at first, but that was mostly my own paranoia. It was fairly easy to get a dorm through OEAD. I know other people who lived in places rented through HousingAnywhere, so that can work. WG's (shared housing, renting a flat with other people) are also great options, but the sites are in german.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: There is no living "on campus" at BOKU, so everyone lives off campus. Do not be intimidated if you live a bit far from campus, focus on being close to the center (and on the good side of the river, which means not Floridsdorf). The public transport system in Vienna (during the day) is amazing and biking is also possible.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you choose to live in a OEAD Guesthouse, you need to know that it is not like a danish dorm, more like a student hotel. They will charge you for cleaning (a cleaning lady comes every week), they will give you everything you need, but there are almost no parties like we know them and they charge for overnight guests and expect peace and quiet. So, not a partyplace.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The fact that you have to be physically present before you can register and choose your courses sucks.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The process in itself was easy enough, you book an appointment and show up and pay.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Read on the webpage for incoming students and call your coordinator if you need help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I managed to register for all of my classes because I was ridiculously early in Vienna (3 weeks prior to the start), but I think it would have been fine if I came later. Excursions and labwork books up fast.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It seems weird that you have to be there in person, but you get used to it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The academic level intimidated me a bit at first because I had to give a lot of presentations and memorize a lot of things (closed book exams = you need to memorize everything), but it turned out to be fine. Be aware that levels vary a lot and some classes do not correspond to the ECTS you get for them (goes both ways, some are harder, some are easier)

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Overall, fairly easy level. But the
system...most
courses are 3 ECTS, so you end up taking 10 courses in a semester, some has multiple exams and there is no structure in schedule, so everything overlaps. A lot.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: As mentioned, completely different system. Much freer, teachers were more easy-going (and answered emails really fast), but not structure. Overlaps everywhere, you are really on your own. Almost no reading in most of my classes, it was just about being there in person and take notes. Seminars are seminars YOU give (important to know). It feels like they have taken courses and split them into different parts: lectures, excursions, seminars, labwork.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Python for beginners, Gender, nutrition and right to food, biotechnology for sustainable innovation and environmental protection, Food biotechnology, German internsive course, German for beginners II,Molecular biology of fungi, genetic modified organisms in the environment, food packaging technology,

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The foodpackaging course was surprisingly good I would say. And gender, nutrition and right to food is very interesting because it is completely different from any other course I have had.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Get an austrian phone subscription, your danish one will stop working (google fair use policy)

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transport was very very cheap and so was going out (beer)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Join the events from the ESN Network in the beginning and try a USI class. I did ballroom dancing, which is a big thing in Vienna, and met nice people.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Everything. A lot of different sports, music and different parties and trips.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I recommend going out and trying things in the beginning, but don't try to do everything (like I did). You can't, there is just too much.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: If you like hiking, bring your hiking gear. I didn't and I regretted it.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy. The culture is a bit more old-fashioned (cash, paper, conservative), but still very european. The language barrier was real though, since I spoke zero german before I went there.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join USI classes and talk to people in class. It is very very easy to stay in the "Erasmus bubble" with all the other exchange students (but that is also fun). Oh, and Tinder. If you are single, that is a very  very easy way to meet local people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Their insistance on using paper, cash and physical, pre-booked appointments for everything.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: That there was also something happening. If you want, you can find a new place to explore every night all days of the week. The raves were fun too. The dancing and the fact that people just know how to do that was also cool.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be prepared for having to send the same information multiple times (but people are nice)
2. The courses will seem like a complete mess because the system is nothing like here, but it will work out, I promise.
3. Vienna is amazing and has a lot of opportunities.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Book more courses than you need, always attend the first class (otherwise you get kicked out of the course) and then drop the ones you don't want afterwards. BOKU has sort of a "trying out" period, so you are not bound to the courses for the first times there.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: There were so many parts. Living in a bigger city, meeting new cultures and subcultures, new people from all over the world, gaining academic confidence by taking classes outside my own field.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The bureaucracy. If you are gone for longer than six months or sublet your place, please please please prepare yourself to be kicked out of the danish system. I had to deal with A LOT of stuff suddenly because I no longer had a permanent danish address. And I thought I was prepared. It works out in the end, it will be okay, but the experience was not fun.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
